content: A nightmare is a type of dream that elicits a strong and unpleasant emotional response from the individual experiencing it. These emotions are often characterized by intense fear or horror, but they can also include sensations such as pain, falling, drowning, or even death. Nightmares may arise due to physical factors, such as a high fever, or psychological factors, such as trauma or stress in the individual’s life. In some cases, nightmares may occur without any identifiable cause. For individuals who have undergone psychologically traumatic events—such as being captured and tortured—the distressing experience may resurface in the form of nightmares. These dreams can be so vivid and distressing that they cause the sleeper to awaken in a state of significant emotional distress, often making it difficult for them to return to sleep for an extended period. While occasional nightmares are a common phenomenon, recurrent nightmares can disrupt sleep patterns and may prompt individuals to seek medical intervention. A recently developed therapeutic approach known as imagery rehearsal therapy has shown promise in mitigating the effects of nightmares. This technique has also demonstrated efficacy in alleviating symptoms associated with acute stress disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Additionally, practitioners of lucid dreaming suggest that this skill can help individuals confront and overcome certain types of nightmares, though it may not be effective for all forms of nightmares. Historically, the term nightmare originally referred to a state now recognized as sleep paralysis, which is often associated with rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. This definition was formalized by Dr. Samuel Johnson in his A Dictionary of the English Language. Early interpretations of nightmares, as understood by figures such as Erasmus Darwin and Henry Fuseli, described them as a morbid oppression during sleep, likened to the sensation of a heavy weight pressing on the chest. In earlier times, nightmares were frequently attributed to supernatural causes, such as the actions of demons or malevolent spirits. Specifically, the incubus was believed to sit on the chests of sleepers, causing the oppressive sensations. In Old English, these entities were referred to as mare or mære, derived from the Proto-Germanic term marōn, which is also related to Old High German and Old Norse terms for similar beings. This etymology is the origin of the mare in the word nightmare. Folklore from regions such as Newfoundland, South Carolina, and Georgia describes a similar phenomenon involving a malevolent entity known as the Hag. According to these beliefs, the Hag leaves her physical body at night and sits on the chest of her victim, inducing sleep paralysis. In Gullah folklore, this experience is referred to as being hag-ridden. The Old Hag was a prominent figure in British and Anglo-American folklore, often described as a nightmare spirit. In addition to supernatural explanations, various forms of magic and spiritual possession were also proposed as causes of nightmares. In 19th-century Europe, dietary habits and irregularities were also thought to contribute to the occurrence of nightmares.
